description:
Start with a real project

Choose a market, device and small list of queries. Assign each query to a page and write down why it matters.

Review the first version

Compare rank changes with Search Console clicks and impressions where available. Check the actual results when the ranking page changes.

Check the final result

Run an audit after major edits and sort issues by their effect on key URLs. Confirm plan limits before building a recurring report.

Frequently asked questions

Why might rank data differ from Search Console?

The settings, query mix and measurement methods can differ. Compare results over a meaningful period with the market and device in mind.

Browse related tools on [SEOGBTools](https://seogbtools.com/).

Use one ranking change to decide what to investigate

Choose a tracked query and the page you expect to appear. If a different page begins showing up, open both pages and look at the search results in the tracked market. A guide and a product listing may cover the same phrase while answering different questions. Check whether the page that appears helps the reader with the task shown in the results.

Compare the change over several observations and record relevant site edits. Search Console can add clicks and impressions for the same query and page when data is available. Check the country and device before comparing the numbers. If the pages cover the same question, clarify what each one is for and add internal links where readers would benefit from moving between them.

Should I rewrite a page after a single position drop?

Check which URL appears, how long the change lasts, and whether relevant clicks or impressions moved. A pattern gives you a clearer reason to edit.

**Public keyword candidates** SE Ranking group buy, keyword rank tracker, website audit, competitor keyword analysis.

Set up an SE Ranking project around the right pages

Start with a list of the URLs that matter to your business. A small store might pick its homepage, two key categories, and three product pages. Give each page a few phrases that match what someone can do there. A search for running shoe size advice could belong to a guide. A search for a specific shoe model could belong to the matching product page.

Decide where you want to measure rankings. Keep the market and device consistent when you compare dates. A mobile result in one city answers a different question from a desktop result across a whole country. For local work, record the target location alongside the keyword. Include the page you expect to rank so you can spot when a different page appears.

Connect the keyword rank tracker with Search Console

Use tracked positions to observe a consistent set of searches. Use Google Search Console to check the impressions and clicks Google recorded for your own site. For example, a rank tracker might show that your category page moved from position 14 to 10 for one phrase. Search Console can help show whether visits rose for that page or whether most impressions came from other phrases.

When a position changes, look at more than one check before making a major edit. Review the ranking URL and the other results for the query. If a guide starts appearing for a buying phrase, check whether your product or category page gives shoppers enough useful detail. Also check your internal links. The guide can direct readers to the relevant buying page where it fits the topic.

Use the website audit to plan fixes

Choose representative pages before reading the whole audit. Open a homepage, category, product, and article. Confirm the issue in a browser or in the page markup where appropriate. If many pages show the same problem, check whether they share a template. One change to a menu or category template may fix many affected URLs.

Prioritize issues by what they stop a visitor or search engine from doing. A broken link in the main navigation deserves a closer look because it can affect many journeys. A description that could be clearer on one old article is a different kind of task. Assign each fix to someone and record how they will check it after the update. Run another crawl and compare the same pages before closing the task.

Review competitors for topics your site can cover

Pick sites that show up for the same searches, even when they are different from the businesses you compete with offline. Use Competitive Research to examine which pages and keywords appear in its estimates. Then open the public pages. Look at what they help a reader do. A competitor may provide sizing advice, a comparison table, or a detailed buying guide that answers questions your page leaves open.

Choose gaps that fit your own business. If a competitor ranks for a topic outside your service area, skip it. For relevant topics, add information you can verify, such as real product dimensions, examples from your own work, or answers your team gives to customers. Use competing pages to see the questions buyers ask and write the answers from your own knowledge.

Compare SE Ranking access before ordering

Test the tasks you repeat each week. Check whether you can track the locations and devices you need, crawl enough pages for your project, and export reports in the format you use. Compare those details with the access offered by SEOGBTools and with a direct subscription if you need team permissions or private client reporting. Keep client credentials and private data in accounts that your team manages.

Build a keyword map for one part of your website

Start with one category or service area. List the pages that belong to it and what visitors can do on each page. Add a small set of queries next to each page. Put buying searches against product or category pages where that makes sense. Give questions about setup, use, or selection to guides that answer them. This map lets you see when two pages are trying to serve the same search and where a useful page is missing.

For example, a store might sell desk lamps and publish a guide about choosing lighting for video calls. The category should help a buyer see the available lamps and compare them. The guide should answer questions about glare, light placement, and adjustable brightness. Link from the guide to the category when you explain which features to look for. If visitors need a lamp that clips to a monitor, the guide can point to a matching product with details that support the recommendation.

Review the map with the person who knows the site's products or services. They may tell you that a popular phrase implies a feature the business does not offer. Keep those queries out of the main tracking list unless you have a reason to monitor them. A list of accurate phrases tied to useful pages is easier to act on than a large export of loosely related words.

Set a baseline before changing the website

Save the date, market, search engine, device, tracked phrases, and expected URLs. Record what is currently live on the pages you plan to edit. A baseline can be as simple as the existing title, the primary heading, and links from related pages. For a larger change, include a crawl of the affected section. When you review results later, you will know what changed and what was already present.

Make a note of other changes that can affect the comparison. A product might go out of stock, a seasonal campaign might end, or a new page might appear above yours. A ranking report can show that a position moved. The project notes can help you explain why several different changes happened around the same time. Keep the report factual and identify the parts that still need checking.

Choose a small group of pages that you can improve and verify. If you edit fifty pages in one afternoon, a shift in traffic may be difficult to trace. A limited release gives you a clearer set of pages to monitor. When you do need a sitewide release, save examples of each affected template so you can compare their status and links after the release.

Investigate a ranking change at the page level

First check whether the same URL ranks for the keyword before and after the change. If a different page replaced it, open both pages and compare their purpose. The new result may be a better match. It may also be a thin tag page or an old guide that sends visitors to the wrong place. Confirm that the intended URL works, can be reached through links, and contains the information a reader would expect.

Next, look at related queries. One keyword can move on its own while the page continues to earn steady clicks across many other phrases. If several relevant terms drop together, examine recent edits, page availability, and the pages that moved up. Use Search Console if you have access to check what happened to the page's recorded clicks and impressions. Look at a period with enough data for a fair comparison.

Finally, decide what would justify an edit. A temporary movement after a small update may only need monitoring. A product page replaced by a retired URL may need a technical fix. A page that attracts visitors for a different purpose might need clearer copy or a better link from a related guide. Write down what you observed and what you expect the next change to improve.

Use a site audit after a store migration

Imagine a store moves its buying guides into a new section and changes the paths of several product categories. Before release, list the old URLs and the intended destinations. Include links from popular articles, the main menu, and the sitemap. That list gives you a practical set of URLs to test even if the full site has thousands of pages.

After release, check the old paths and follow them through to the final page. If an old category points to a page with a different purpose, choose a closer destination where possible. Update the menu and key articles to link directly to the current page. Review the sitemap and canonical information for the new URLs. A crawl can surface patterns, but a manual check confirms what a person sees on important pages.

Group issues by cause. If a filter creates extra URLs, check where those links appear and what the site's plan is for filtered pages. If old guide URLs remain in the menu, fix the menu entry and check a few pages that use it. When the issue comes from a template, give the developer one clear task with several examples. Rerun the audit and confirm that the sampled pages now behave as expected.

Turn competitor research into an original page brief

Choose competitors that appear for the phrases you actually want to serve. A national marketplace might be useful for seeing how buyers compare products. A specialist shop might be more useful for understanding how buyers choose between models. Record which page you reviewed and what question it answers. Review the public content because an estimated keyword list alone does not tell you whether a page is useful.

Write down missing details your own team can supply. A desk lamp guide might need examples of where to place a lamp in a small room. A category page might need filters for mounting style, brightness settings, or price. A product page might benefit from a photo that shows the power connector or clamp size. Choose details that solve a genuine shopping problem and that you can verify using the item.

Build the brief around the visitor's next step. For an educational guide, the next step might be measuring a desk or learning where to position a light. For a category, it might be comparing two styles. For a product, it might be confirming the mount fits and placing an order. Add internal links when they help the reader do something the current page cannot complete on its own.

Make a weekly report that leads to decisions

Report the pages and keywords you agreed to track, the changes that matter, and the next action. A short note might say that the category gained visibility for two product terms, but the buying guide still ranks for one phrase intended for the category. Include a link to both pages and what you plan to check. A reader can act on that without sorting through a spreadsheet of daily position changes.

Give each technical issue a clear owner. For example, an editor can improve an article title, a developer can fix a menu link that appears across templates, and a product manager can confirm details needed for a comparison table. Record how each task will be verified. A broken link fix can be checked by opening the source and following the updated link. A new product detail can be checked against the actual item.

Record what is still uncertain. A higher tracked position may show up before there is enough click data for a meaningful comparison. A crawl may find an issue that only appears with one set of filters. Document those details so that the next report can confirm them. Over time, this creates a record of what you changed, what happened, and how you chose the next improvement.

Compare SEO platforms using the same task

If you are comparing SE Ranking with Semrush or Ahrefs, choose one project and give each tool the same job. Track a short list of queries for the same market, inspect a section of a site, or identify a few pages from one competitor. Look at the context each tool provides, the limits of the plan you are evaluating, and how easily another person could repeat your work.

Make separate notes for measurement and research. A rank tracker follows chosen queries under set conditions. Competitive research tools can help you find new terms and pages to inspect. A site crawl focuses on how the website works. If you mostly need to see which searches already send traffic to your own site, include Search Console in that comparison. Choose the combination that answers your team's recurring questions.

How many keywords should I start with?

Start with enough to cover the pages you intend to improve and the markets you serve. Give each phrase an expected page and a reason to track it. Add more phrases when you have a question they can answer. Remove or pause terms that no longer match the products or services you offer.

What should I do if two URLs appear for one keyword?

Check what each page offers. Similar pages may need clearer roles and better internal links. Pages with different purposes can both be useful when the search has mixed intent. Look at the actual search results and at your own data before deciding whether to update a page or combine overlapping content.

Can a website audit confirm that Google indexed a page?

A crawl can help you inspect signals such as links, response codes, and directives. Use Google's URL Inspection report, where you have access, to check Google's reported status for a specific URL. If you make a fix, verify the live page and allow time for Google to process the change.
